summary: A brick light (1855) on Baker Island in the Cranberry Isles, first lit in 1828 with William Gilley, whose family had settled the island, as keeper.

structures.note: Replaced an 1828 rubblestone tower. Height sources differ: 43 ft to lantern centre (US Lighthouse Society), 37 ft to focal plane (nomination), 45 ft (LighthouseFriends).
L-shaped clapboard dwelling; a kitchen wing was added about 1868 (LighthouseFriends).

access.note: Owned by the National Park Service (tower acquired 2011). No dock: small craft only. No public access inside the tower. Views from the water or on guided tours; the ranger-led boat cruise ended in 2024.

facts.agency: National Park Service, Acadia National Park (owner); US Coast Guard maintains the light as an aid to navigation

events.note: The Gilley family settled the island about 1812 (Eliot); the park gives about 1806.
Rubblestone tower and keeper's dwelling built, $3,800 (LighthouseFriends).
First light; William Gilley appointed keeper at $350 a year.
Lewis inspection found the tower and dwelling cracked (LighthouseFriends).
Gilley removed as keeper after the Whig party took power (Eliot dates 1849; LighthouseFriends 1848).
Brick tower and dwelling built to replace the 1828 station; $4,963 (LighthouseFriends).
Fourth-order Fresnel lens installed.
Crew of the schooner Challenge, sunk near Petit Manan, landed on Baker's Island; taken off by Station No. 4 the next morning.
Brig Shamrock ran ashore in fog on the northwest part of Baker's Island; floated off 22 January.
Brick oil house built.
Telephone line to Northeast Harbor completed (Lighthouse Board fiscal 1899; LighthouseFriends gives 1898).
Reinforcement of the tower; the nature is unclear (nomination).
Fuel house built.
Illuminant changed to incandescent oil vapor.
Deactivated November 1955 (LighthouseFriends).
Reactivated April 1957 as an unattended aid; US Lighthouse Society gives 1957 as the automation year.
Station except the tower transferred from the Coast Guard to the National Park Service.
The park's page gives 1966 for automation.
Listed on the National Register of Historic Places, March 14, 1988.
Coast Guard proposed discontinuing the light in 1991 and again in 1997; local protests kept it lit.
The tower was acquired by the National Park Service.
Solar-powered Vega VLB-44 LED optic installed.
Friends of Acadia raised more than $400,000 toward restoring the tower (August 2026).

notes_for_editor: 1. Settlement year: Eliot gives about 1812 (followed in the story); the park's Baker Island page gives about 1806; LighthouseFriends gives 1812. Both stated. 2. Removal of William Gilley: Eliot gives 1849, LighthouseFriends 1848 (the USLHS roster says 1849). Both stated. 3. First station: LighthouseFriends describes a rubblestone tower of 1828; the park's lighthouses page says stone; the park's Baker Island page says 'the original wooden structure'. Not reconciled; the story states the park's wording and LighthouseFriends' description. 4. Tower height: see resolved_conflicts. 5. Automation: 1957 (USLHS) against 1966 (park), and the light was reactivated April 1957 after deactivation November 1955 (LighthouseFriends). 6. Telephone: 1898 (LighthouseFriends) against the fiscal 1899 Lighthouse Board report. 7. Lens: on display at the Fisherman's Museum, Pemaquid Point (LighthouseFriends, which also says the lens is 'now in' it). Not verified with the museum. 8. The 1880 and 1882 rescue entries were checked against the report text on the cited scan pages (1880 p. 129; 1882 p. 163). Both cited pages were confirmed by corpus.py page. The 1880 Challenge's distance is 'about five miles south of Petit Manan light'; the report does not say nautical miles, so none is given. 9. Other 'Baker's Island' entries (the LSS 1880 list has 'Baker's Island Shoals, Mass.'; the Bulletin index lists a Massachusetts 'Bakers Island' station) are not used. 10. Keepers: LighthouseFriends describes family events of keepers Joseph Muise and others (a 1932 drowning, a birth in a lifeboat); these are private family matters and are not used. 11. The Gilley sons' claim and the nineteen-acre award rest on LighthouseFriends alone; attributed in the story. 12. The record's 'Fl W 10s' and 10 nm range are not in any source read; left out of facts. 13. The record's tower (conical masonry, 1828) does not match the NRHP or USLHS (cylindrical brick, 1855); see corrections. 14. Eliot's book: the Applewood reprint (Internet Archive full text) says first published in The Century Magazine in 1899 and in book form in 1904; the story's footnote gives 1904. Quotations carry no page numbers in the reprint text. 15. The 1912 illuminant change is from the Lighthouse Service Bulletin 1912, PDF p. 47 (the item lists Baker Island among the changes; the Bulletin does not date it more precisely). 16. Alden H. Jordan: the same USLHS person slug (alden-h-jordan) appears on the Baker Island (1867-1883) and Bear Island (1883-1899) rosters, so the other_stations link is supported by USLHS. 17. Howard Bryant Clement is listed under a USCG heading in the USLHS roster; role recorded as 'other' with a note. 18. The NRHP's 1903 reinforcement is described in LighthouseFriends as an external four-inch brick wall; the story gives both.

corrections.why: The nomination describes a cylindrical brick tower; the US Lighthouse Society record gives 'CYLINDRICAL'.
The standing brick tower was built in 1855; the 1828 tower was rubblestone and was replaced.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Eliot gives 1849 for William Gilley's removal after the Whig party came to power; LighthouseFriends gives 1848. The story states both and does not choose.
Eliot and LighthouseFriends date the Gilley family's move to about 1812; the park's Baker Island page says about 1806. The story follows Eliot, the primary family account, and states the difference.
LighthouseFriends dates the Northeast Harbor telephone line to 1898; the Lighthouse Board's report for the fiscal year ended June 30, 1899 says it was completed. Both are stated.
USLHS gives 1957 (the year the light was reactivated as an unattended aid, per LighthouseFriends); the park gives 1966. Both stated.
43 ft to the centre of the lantern (USLHS), 37 ft to the lens focal plane (NRHP), 45 ft for the brick tower (LighthouseFriends). These measure different points; the story states all three.
